newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch closing debt market report.
newsitem.headline: Dutch closing debt market report.

text.p: Dutch bonds ended the first day of the new week mixed after a session of thin, range-bound trade.
Most guilder bonds opened higher in a belated reaction to Friday's U.S. economic data, but a general lack of interest caused most earlier gains to fade away at midsession.
Toward the end of trade, U.S. January NAPM, which came in below expectations at 52, lifted the market somewhat without sparking heavy trade.
"Most players will stay sidelined until the FOMC has made its announcements," said a dealer, explaining the quiet market.
The Federal Reserve's Open Market Committe (FOMC) will meet on Tuesday and Wednesday and, although most traders do not expect a rate hike on this occasion, the market is careful.
"You never know, a surprise always remains possible," a trader worded market sentiment.
The 6.25 July 1998 Dutch bond ended three basis points lower at a price of 104.03/11, yielding 3.32 percent at bid.
September 2001s closed 0.03 higher at 117.33/43, for a bid yield of 4.49 percent.
The 5.75 Feb 2007 bond, the new 10-year benchmark, added 0.11 to 100.77/87, yielding 5.65 percent.
But the 10-year yield spread versus the January 2007 Bund was steady at minus six basis points.
Among the long bonds, the Dutch January 2023s closed at 114.10/30, for a 6.37 percent yield, versus 113.85/114.05.
The 30-year yield spread versus January 2024 Bunds narrowed 0.01 to 18 basis points.

Separately, ABN Amro said in a research note it expected the long-term interest differential with Germany to remain negative in 1997. It expects German long-term interest rates to edge up to 6.25 percent at the end of 1997, while the Dutch equivalent was seen rising to 6.10 percent.

The bank cited the comparatively good shape of the Dutch government finances, the low Dutch borrowing requirement and the upcoming narrowing of the inflation differential between the two countries due to the harmonisation of inflation figures.
